newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - Kodak sees rump copier units profitable.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Kodak sees rump copier units profitable.

text.p: Eastman Kodak Co will keep copier-related businesses with yearly sales of $600 million and expects the units to be operationally profitable by the end of 1997, a top Kodak executive said on Monday.
Kodak earlier announced the $684 million sale of its copier-distribution and services businesses to Danka Business Systems Plc.

Those units have sales of about $1.2 billion, and the agreed transaction came after a nine-month campaign by Kodak's top managers to divest or strategically reposition its businesses in a segment dominated by Xerox Corp.
"We will retain all of the manufacturing," Kodak co-chief operating officer Carl Kohrt told Reuters.

Under the deal, expected to close by December 31, Danka will acquire Kodak's sales, marketing and equipment-services operations and will become the biggest customer for Kodak's copiers and research-and-development enterprises in copiers.
Danka will also take over Kodak's business which runs mailrooms and copier operations for other companies.
"We expect by the end of 1997 to have sustained profitability," Kohrt said of the remaining copier units.
Kodak also said it expects the deal to immediately add to earnings, once completed. Kodak will take a book of about $250 million after taxes and receive net cash of about $600 million from the sale.

Monday's deal is just the latest bit of corporate trimming at Kodak, which has spun off and sold businesses, generating some $8 billion. The company has in the 1990s exited pharmaceuticals, household goods and chemicals.

Chief executive George Fisher, in office since late 1993, is directing the company towards digital imaging businesses and increasing sales of Kodak's highly profitable traditional film in Asia, Latin America and other areas outside the United States.

Analyst Gary Schneider of Bear Stearns said he had hoped Kodak would have quit copies entirely and will have to prove to Wall Street it can turn around the financial performance of the remaining copier businesses. Kodak has long been an also-ran against segement leader Xerox Corp
"The question is what kind of normalized earnings can you get out of those," he said.
Kohrt said the deal with Danka will stimulate sales of Kodak copiers. "What we've really needed is pull-through from the market," he said.
Danka chief executive Dan Doyle said Kodak's strong focus on big customers needing high-volume copiers and services dovetailed with Danka's traditional presence among low and middle-market customers.

Schneider discounted the significance of Kodak's statement earnings would be helped immediately by the sale. Interest payments alone on $600 million would be sufficient to do that, he said, and speculated the money may be used to fund or expand Kodak's on-going stock repurchases.
